sections.content:
Seeing your favourite artist live is one of the best experiences you can have — but paying £50 more than someone sitting three rows away? That stings long after the encore.

The reality is that concert ticket prices vary significantly depending on where you buy them. The same seat for the same show can cost noticeably more on one platform than another, and with booking fees, service charges, and delivery costs layered on top, it is easy to pay far more than you need to. This guide walks you through exactly how to compare concert ticket prices across platforms, so you can confidently get the best deal — and spend what you save on the merch stand.

sections.title: Why Concert Ticket Prices Vary Across Platforms
sections.content:
Before diving into how to compare, it helps to understand *why* the same ticket can carry such different price tags depending on where you look.

**Resale vs. face value.** Primary ticketing sites like Ticketmaster and AXS sell tickets at the official face value set by the venue or promoter. Resale marketplaces — such as StubHub, Viagogo, and Twickets — list tickets from fans who have already bought them, often at a markup (or occasionally at a discount if the event is approaching and sellers need to shift their seats quickly).

**Platform fees.** Almost every ticketing platform adds a service or booking fee at checkout, and these can range from a modest 10% to an eye-watering 30% or more on top of the listed price. Two platforms showing the same face value can result in very different totals by the time you click confirm.

**Dynamic pricing.** Increasingly, primary platforms use dynamic pricing, meaning ticket prices rise as demand increases — much like airline seats. A ticket that cost £60 in the first sale window may be £120 by the time it reaches the top of the queue.

**Delivery and fulfilment costs.** Print-at-home or mobile tickets are usually free to deliver; physical tickets can add another £3–£8 to the total.

None of this is hidden — but it is scattered across a dozen different websites, making meaningful price comparison time-consuming to do manually.

sections.title: How to Compare Concert Ticket Prices Manually
sections.content: If you want to do the legwork yourself, here is a reliable approach.

sections.title: 1. Start with the official tour or artist website
sections.content: Most artists link to authorised ticketing partners from their own website. This tells you where face-value tickets are available and which platforms are officially endorsed. Starting here helps you avoid accidental purchases from fraudulent secondary listings.

sections.title: 2. Check the primary ticketing platforms
sections.content:
Search for the event on the major primary sellers relevant to your region:

- **UK:** Ticketmaster, AXS, See Tickets, Gigantic, Dice
- **US:** Ticketmaster, Live Nation, AXS, Eventbrite
- **EU:** Eventim, Fnac, See Tickets

Note the *total* price at checkout — not the headline price — including all fees. A £70 ticket with a £22 booking fee is actually £92.

sections.title: 3. Check the resale marketplaces
sections.content: If primary tickets are sold out or you are after a different area of the venue, search secondary marketplaces such as StubHub, Viagogo, and Twickets. Filter by the seat section you want and again note the total checkout price, including any buyer protection fees.

sections.title: 4. Build a simple comparison
sections.content:
Open a spreadsheet (or just a notes app) and log the following:

| Platform | Ticket price | Fees | Total | Delivery |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ticketmaster | £65 | £13 | £78 | Free |
| See Tickets | £65 | £8.50 | £73.50 | Free |
| StubHub | £85 | £17 | £102 | Free |

The cheapest platform is rarely obvious from the headline price alone.

sections.title: 5. Verify before you buy
sections.content:
Before purchasing from a resale site, check:

- Whether the platform offers a buyer guarantee (protection if the ticket is invalid or the event is cancelled)
- The seller's rating and history
- Whether the ticket will arrive before the event date

This process works — but it takes 20–30 minutes per event, across multiple tabs, and you still risk missing a platform that had the best price. Which is where a dedicated comparison tool changes the picture entirely.

sections.title: The Smarter Way: Use Tour Ticket Compare
sections.content:
Tour Ticket Compare does the comparison for you. Rather than manually visiting five or six platforms, you search for your artist or event once, and Tour Ticket Compare pulls live prices from across the major ticketing sites in a single view.

This means you can see at a glance which platform is offering the best total price for the seats you want — without opening multiple tabs, recalculating fees, or worrying that you have missed a better deal elsewhere.

The tool is particularly useful when:

- **Tickets are available across multiple platforms** and prices differ meaningfully between them
- **A tour is just announced** and you want to move quickly without sacrificing comparison speed
- **You are flexible on seating** and want to see where the best value in each section sits
- **Fees are a concern** — Tour Ticket Compare surfaces total prices, not just face values, so you are comparing like for like

sections.title: What to Watch Out for When Comparing Prices
sections.content:
Even with a comparison tool, a few things are worth keeping in mind.

**Total price is the only price that matters.** Always confirm the full checkout total before assuming one platform is cheaper. Headline prices without fees are not a fair comparison.

**Resale tickets carry risk.** Platforms with buyer guarantees are preferable when purchasing from the secondary market. If a listing looks unusually cheap, treat it with caution.

**Timing affects price.** Prices on resale markets tend to drop in the week leading up to a show as sellers become motivated. If you are flexible and comfortable with a little risk, waiting can pay off — but popular events can also sell out entirely, so it is a calculated gamble.

**Section and row matter.** A lower total price in the back of the floor may be worse value than a slightly higher price with an unobstructed seated view, depending on the venue and how you prefer to experience live music. Price comparison works best when you are comparing equivalent seating categories.

sections.title: Tips to Get the Best Concert Ticket Deal
sections.content:
- **Set alerts where available.** Some platforms allow you to register interest or set a price alert for an event, notifying you when tickets become available or drop in price.
- **Check multiple seating sections.** Sometimes adjacent sections to the main floor or premium areas offer nearly the same experience at a fraction of the price.
- **Buy in the first sale window.** For high-demand artists, primary ticket prices increase with demand. Buying in the first minutes of sale — at face value — is almost always cheaper than waiting.
- **Use a comparison tool every time.** Even for artists you follow closely and buy tickets for regularly, the platform with the best price changes from tour to tour. Comparing takes seconds with the right tool; the savings can be significant.
- **Factor in travel and timing.** If two venues on a tour are similarly priced but one requires overnight accommodation, the true cost is very different.

sections.title: FAQ
sections.content:
**Why is the same concert ticket cheaper on some sites than others?**

Ticket prices vary because of platform booking fees, whether a site is a primary seller (selling at face value) or a secondary marketplace (resale), and dynamic pricing models that adjust based on demand. The headline price is rarely the final price — fees at checkout are where most of the variation actually lies.

**Is it safe to buy concert tickets from resale platforms?**

Reputable resale platforms such as StubHub and Twickets offer buyer guarantees that protect you if a ticket is invalid or an event is cancelled. Smaller or unverified resellers carry more risk. Always use platforms with a formal buyer protection policy and check seller ratings before purchasing.

**What is the best site to buy concert tickets?**

There is no single best site — it depends on the event, the artist, and when you are buying. The most reliable approach is to compare prices across primary and secondary platforms for your specific event and date. A tool like Tour Ticket Compare lets you do this in one search rather than visiting each platform individually.

**How do I avoid booking fees on concert tickets?**

Booking fees are charged by almost all ticketing platforms and are rarely avoidable entirely. Some platforms charge lower fees than others for the same event, which is why comparing total checkout prices — not just face values — is essential. Occasionally, buying directly from a venue box office in person avoids online service fees.

**When is the cheapest time to buy concert tickets?**

For primary tickets, buying during the initial sale window is usually cheapest, as dynamic pricing increases costs as demand grows. For resale tickets, prices often soften in the days immediately before a show. For high-demand events, however, tickets may sell out entirely — so waiting carries real risk.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.content:
Concert ticket prices are not fixed, and the gap between the cheapest and most expensive platform for the same seat can easily reach £30–£50 or more once fees are included. The good news is that with a clear comparison process — or better yet, a tool like Tour Ticket Compare — finding the best deal is straightforward.
